extracted.intended_audience: online educators, instructional designers, e-learning researchers, and higher-education teachers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for designing, assessing, and theorizing online/e-learning environments, with emphasis on learner, knowledge, assessment, and community lenses and on interaction modalities. Useful for course designers, instructors, and researchers developing online courses or studying online pedagogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions of a good educational theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Wilson (1997) describes three functions of a good educational theory: (1) helps us to envision new worlds; (2) helps us to make things (invest time/resources effectively); (3) keeps us honest (builds on what is known and constrains day-to-day contingencies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theory should both inspire novel uses of technology and ground practical design decisions; it should guide resource allocation (efficiency) and ensure robustness and growth of practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learner-Centred (learning-centred) design
rubrics_metrics.description: Awareness of learners’ unique cognitive structures, prerequisite knowledge, and misconceptions; respect for cultural attributes, language, and forms of expression; use of diagnostic tools to reveal pre-existing knowledge structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In online contexts, provide time at course start for students to share understandings (electronically administered surveys, virtual icebreakers), probe for Internet efficacy, and scaffold technology competence; recognize 'learner-centred' often implies balancing individual needs with teacher/institutional/societal constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge-Centred learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective learning is defined and bounded by the epistemology, language, and context of disciplinary thought; instruction must allow students to experience discipline-specific discourse and knowledge structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachers should provide big-picture scaffolding to help students navigate abundant web resources; support reflective capacity so automacy is complemented by transfer and new knowledge construction (apply discipline-grounded tasks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment-Centred design
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning environments must be assessment-centred—emphasising formative evaluation and summative assessment that inform, motivate, and provide feedback to learners and teachers rather than relying solely on high-stakes recall testing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design assessments aligned with content and cognitive processes (e.g., coherent explanations, planning, implementation, monitoring/adjusting). Use peer/expert review and self-assessment; avoid predominance of recall questions; consider process-assessment opportunities in project/workplace-based tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community-Centred learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning should be community-centred: social components (shared belonging, trust, expectation of learning, commitment) support collaborative knowledge construction (community of inquiry/practice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize barriers in online communities (placedness, anonymity, synchronicity). Accommodate diverse participation expectations and life-stage needs; adapt formats to balance independence and community participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access to technology as a design criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider access: Web access is widespread in many contexts but remains problematic for some (physical handicaps, limited connectivity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design assuming broadly increasing access but explicitly address accessibility and inclusion (alternate formats, assistive tech).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abundance of content and the need for filtering
rubrics_metrics.description: The Web provides an era of abundant content (open journals, OERs, blogs, huge searchable resources) which can overwhelm learners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Course design must include mechanisms to filter, curate, and scaffold content selection—reducing choice overload is as important as providing content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multimodality / media selection
rubrics_metrics.description: The Web supports many media (text, streaming video, audio conferencing, immersive worlds); different media have different affordances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose technological options best suited to your learning outcomes; earlier techniques optimized text-based interaction, but richer media may be better for some tasks while restricting independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperlinking and constructivist learning paths
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyperlinking aligns with human mental schema and supports constructivist discovery—allowing students to create personal learning paths through linked resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage hypertext to support exploration but provide scaffolding so learners construct coherent knowledge structures rather than get lost in links.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ease of content update and responsiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: The Web makes content easy to update and revise (blogs, CMSs like Blackboard/Moodle), enabling more current, responsive materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance benefits of rapid updates with risks: potential for error and uneven professional quality. Establish editorial/quality-control practices where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication/interaction capacity as primary affordance
rubrics_metrics.description: The Web’s greatest educational affordance is its profound and multifaceted increase in communication and interaction capability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design should capitalise on communication channels to support learning communities, feedback, collaboration, and social presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Interaction (Wagner, 2001): 'reciprocal events that require at least two objects and two actions. Interactions occur when these objects and events mutually influence one another.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this reciprocity notion when designing learning activities to ensure meaningful mutual influence among actors/objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions of interactivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Interactivity allows learner control, facilitates program adaptation based on learner input, allows participation/communication, aids meaningful learning, and helps create learning communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design interactive elements that enable control, adaptation, and meaningful engagement rather than superficial interactivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student-Student Interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer-to-peer interaction supports multiple perspectives, collaborative learning gains, higher completion rates, acquisition of social skills, and benefits for both tutor and tutee (reciprocal teaching).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foster student-led teams and peer tutoring to increase cognitive, social, and teaching presence; incorporate collaborative tasks and structures for effective peer engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student-Content Interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Student-content interaction includes passive study (reading) and active immersion (virtual labs, simulations); adaptive content can customize paths based on student modelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide immediate feedback, intelligent help, adaptive interfaces, and model-based navigation suggestions; use interactive content that responds to learner behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student-Teacher Interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Student-teacher interaction in online learning occurs via asynchronous/synchronous text, audio, and video; volume can overwhelm teachers and students may expect immediate responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manage expectations (teachers need not respond instantly to everything), adopt less teacher-centric flows to encourage learner ownership, and design communication patterns that scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher-Content Interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Teachers continuously create, monitor, and update learning objects, units, and associated activities—teacher-content interaction is central to course maintenance and evolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support teachers with authoring tools and workflows that simplify creating/updating resources while maintaining quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher-Teacher Interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Teacher-teacher interaction sustains professional development and support through communities of practice, enabling knowledge growth and pedagogic sharing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage professional communities, shared repositories, and collaborative course development to improve teaching quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content-Content Interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Content-content interaction is automated interaction among content sources (e.g., data feeds), enabling materials to refresh themselves and draw from external services (tagging, RSS/Atom, machine harvesting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design content to leverage syndication and automated updates where appropriate; use tagging and ontologies to enable discovery and rights tracking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction modality tradeoff: richness vs independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Richer communication modalities (face-to-face, video conferencing) support higher interaction but place greater restrictions on independence of time and place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select modalities that balance desired interaction richness with flexibility needs of learners (consider asynchronous/synchronous mixes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalency / substitution of interaction forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Interactions can sometimes be substituted for one another based on cost and accessibility factors (equivalency theorem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing, consider which interactions can be economically or accessibly substituted while preserving learning outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group-as-resource and inclusion of wide networks
rubrics_metrics.description: Groups beyond bounded class membership (responses from strangers, referrals, social networks, virtual-world avatars) can act as educational resources with different characteristics and often more generative potential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate external networks and informal social software as supplementary knowledge resources, while assessing reliability and relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: E-learning models: Collaborative / community-of-inquiry model
rubrics_metrics.description: Community models (collaborative, community-of-inquiry) are rich, support social skills, collaboration, and personal relationships but bind learners in time and are generally more expensive and less scalable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use community models when social learning, discourse, and collaboration are key outcomes; plan for scheduling and higher resource needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: E-learning models: Independent study model
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent study models use structured tools (computer-assisted tutorials, drills, simulations, virtual labs, texts) and permit greater flexibility and scalability while learners may still rely on workplace peers or informal networks for support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use independent models for content/skill acquisition where flexibility is primary; augment with social software to provide optional interaction/support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match learning outcomes to activities (Prensky)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different learning outcomes are best supported by particular learning activities: behaviours via imitation/feedback/practice; creativity via playing; facts via association/drill; judgment via cases/choices/feedback/coaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design activities aligned to the specific 'how do they learn what?' question—choose imitation, play, drill, or case-based activities according to the targeted outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment workload minimization strategies (tools)
rubrics_metrics.description: Strategies and tools to provide formative/summative assessment with minimal teacher workload include: online computer-marked assessments extending to simulations/virtual labs; collaborative student-created documentation; online automated tutors; student agents; project/product-based assessment; machine scoring tools (LSA, neural networks); informal social networks for reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate automated scoring, peer assessment structures, and project-based evaluations to increase assessment quantity/quality without proportionally increasing teacher time; evaluate reliability and validity of automated approaches.
